To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the prevalence of lung cancer among patients who would have met screening criteria was 0.6% and that the prevalence of early stage lung cancer among patients not screened was 0.4% (Table 3).
the prevalence of lung cancer in a screening population is 1.3%, and that 1 in 4 lung cancers detected in a screening population would not have met the current screening criteria.

1) the prevalence of lung cancer in a population of current and former heavy smokers is higher than previously reported and 2) the prevalence of early-stage lung cancer (cT1a or cT1b) in this population is higher than previously thought.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of mathematical models of biological systems and processes.
the development of a new type of computer-aided diagnostic (CAD) system that can assist radiologists to diagnose lung nodules on chest radiographs.
the development and application of mathematical methods in the field of cancer research.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence is insufficient to determine whether lung cancer screening with LDCT in a high-risk population would result in more deaths prevented than lives lost.
the evidence does not support the use of lung cancer screening with low dose CT scans in the general population.

lung cancer screening should be offered to individuals who meet the following criteria: (1) age 55 to 74 years; (2) 30 or more pack-years of cigarette smoking; (3) current smoker or former smoker who quit within the previous 15 years; (4) without a history of prior lung cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the current guidelines are not sensitive and specific enough to identify all patients who will benefit from screening.
the majority of lung cancers are diagnosed in patients who are not eligible for current screening criteria.

we found that 1) a substantial proportion of patients with resected lung cancer in Ontario, Canada, would not have met eligibility for lung cancer screening, and 2) a substantial proportion would have met eligibility for screening, but would have had their lung cancer detected by other means.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the vast majority of lung cancer patients who would have been screened would not have benefited from the screening, and the majority of patients who would benefit from screening would not be screened.
the majority of patients diagnosed with lung cancer would not have met screening criteria.
lung cancer screening is not a one-size-fits-all proposition.
